title: How to Reverse 2.5 Years of Aging in 15 Days (Proven in RCTs)
description: There’s a diet that made people 2.5 years biologically younger in 15 days. Not younger- looking . Younger by a blood test. And when the researchers dug into the numbers, the drop in biological age had little to do with the usual suspects, like how much weight anyone lost. The diet is called the “fasting mimicking diet.” And right now it’s having a moment. Friends corner me about it at holidays. Subscribers bring it up in comment sections across social media. So, today, I’m indulging with you in the science. The human controlled trial data. The nuances that look strange until you understand the biology. And, of course, the “how to.” Specifically, what I ate for five days, what it cost me — about $49 (<$10 per day), versus the $225 they’ll charge you for the branded box. To be clear, I’m not selling you a product, I’ll just show you what’s in my grocery cart. I’ll even tell you about another time I ran a biological-age test on myself and it came back saying I’d gotten older — and what that result reveals about who this actually works for. But let’s start with what a fasting mimicking diet actually is. What is a Fasting Mimicking Diet? First, what is a fasting mimicking diet? The premise is simple. Fasting triggers a remarkable cascade of metabolic changes. But to get many of those effects, you generally need more than daily time-restricted eating. It can take 3 full days of water-only fasting before those deeper metabolic changes begin. That’s the problem because most people aren’t interested in, or able to, fast for three to five straight days.

title: The Mushroom I'm Eating for Brain Health
description: Every now and then, I read a paper that changes what ends up on my dinner plate. This was one of those papers, recently published in Nature Aging . And the food in question is a mushroom, a very particular one. Now, I could spoil its secret identity right now... but what fun would that be? I think you need to earn that information. So let me walk you through the data. The high-level objective was simple: to determine which metabolites in the blood were linked to: Better cognition Greater brain volume Lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease. So, the researchers began by looking for associations between 991 blood metabolites and measures of cognition and brain volume, assessed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) , in 1,082 middle-aged adults. After identifying a subset of metabolites linked to cognition or brain volume, they validated those findings in independent cohorts and then tested whether those same metabolites were also associated with the future development of Alzheimer’s disease. Effectively, they were looking for a coherent story: Which metabolites consistently tracked with better cognition, greater brain volume, and a lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease across multiple populations? But that was only Step 1… Step 2 was to determine which of those metabolites could actually be influenced by modifiable factors such as lifestyle, medications, and diet. That’s how they began to piece the puzzle together. And one molecule rose to the top: Ergothioneine. What is Ergothioneine? Ergothioneine is a sulfur-containing amino acid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. Interestingly, its levels also decline with age , paralleling the gradual loss of antioxidant defenses that occurs as we get older.

title: Your GLP-1 Might Be Turning “ON” Hunger Neurons
description: This might be one of the strangest findings on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs I’ve come across this year. Researchers were studying neurons in the brain that are known to drive hunger. So, you’d expect drugs like semaglutide (Ozempic) to decrease the activity of these cells. Instead, they found the opposite. GLP-1 receptor agonists activated these hunger neurons. You read that right: a drug famous for reducing appetite appeared to switch on the very neurons that drive hunger. Bizarre. Completely paradoxical. What are we missing? And what does this mean if you’re taking a GLP-1? Let’s dive into the science. The Hunger Neurons with a Funny Name First, some quick background. Deep in your brain, nestled in a region called the hypothalamus, sits a cluster of neurons known as AgRP neurons . These cells are your brain’s hunger alarm system. When your energy stores drop or when you skip a meal (if you’re not used to fasting), AgRP neurons fire up. They drive you to seek food. So, the conventional logic goes: If GLP-1 receptor agonists suppress appetite and cause weight loss, they should suppress AgRP neurons. These are hunger cells. The drug kills hunger. So, no duh. Except... that’s not what happened. A new study published in PNAS out of Yale tested this assumption directly. And the results flipped the script. AgRP neurons weren’t suppressed by semaglutide. They were activated by it. What’s more, these neurons were required for the drug’s full weight-lowering effect. But let’s walk through some of the data. What Happens When You Disable the “Hunger Neurons?” The researchers used a clever genetic model. They bred mice in which AgRP neurons were functionally impaired.
